chapter_theme: Once a friend has been chosen, bear their faults: everything has its husk, the patience of one keeps two in friendship, and one who exposes or pries into a friend's faults is worse than the friend.
structure_note: 221 to 226 give images for bearing a chosen friend's wrongs (husk and foam, the dam the stream keeps breaking, fire, the hand that pokes the eye). 227 to 230 turn to exposing a friend's faults, and the chapter ends in a first-person curse on anyone who pries into them.

221.reading: Those one eagerly took as good should be kept close, with their faults held within, even if they prove otherwise; rice has its husk, water its foam, and flowers their rough outer petals.
221.nuance: அடக்கிக் கொளல் can mean holding the friend close or keeping the fault to oneself. Shanmuganar takes the second, and Pope's version has both.

222.reading: Those who live by water don't rage at the fresh flood when it breaks the dam each time they build it, but dam it again; in the same way people bear with those whose bond they sought, even when they do one hateful thing after another.
222.nuance: The friend is needed the way the farmer needs the stream, so here forbearance rests on dependence as much as on goodness.

223.reading: Lord of the high hills where bees hum over the bright kongu flowers, isn't it right to bear with one's friends even when they do great wrong? The patience of one is the friendship of two.
223.nuance: ஒருவர் பொறை இருவர் நட்பு is the maxim: a friendship survives if either party absorbs the injury, so it doesn't need both to be faultless.

224.reading: Lord of the shore where folding waves cast up bright pearls and swift boats rock against the beach, if those one cannot let go lack good nature, they are a fire lit to burn one's heart.
224.nuance: The verse doesn't say to leave them. It names the pain of a bond one cannot leave. Pope's title, about being angry with those we love, is not in the Tamil. Neither commentary is aligned to this quatrain, though Shanmuganar's comment on it appears under 223.

225.reading: Those one ought not to part from must be cherished like gold even when they do harm, since the fire that once destroyed a good house along with its gold is still sought out and kindled at home every day.
225.nuance: Fire both destroys and is needed daily, so the friend is cherished because life needs them, not because the harm is forgotten. Pope takes பொன்னாக as an address to a maiden 'as Lakshmi'; Shanmuganar reads it as 'like gold'.

226.reading: Lord of the sky-piercing hills of rare excellence, is it right to cast off those hard to part from, though they hurt you? Does anyone cut off their own hand because it poked their eye?
226.nuance: The image makes the friend part of one's own body, so cutting them off harms oneself again and undoes nothing.

227.reading: Lord of the cool shore of shining waters, once the worthy have joined with someone they see no fault in them even when hurt; those without firm understanding who bring out another's wrongs after joining with him are themselves lower than he is.
227.nuance: The verse ranks exposing a friend's wrong as worse than the wrong itself.

228.reading: Lord of the land of roaring falls, what is there to grieve over, on reflection, when strangers do great wrong? And what those bound by love have done becomes good when held within the heart.
228.nuance: The same harm is treated by who did it: from a stranger it is to be shrugged off, from one who loves it is to be turned into something good within.

229.reading: If you find that those you took as your own are not, honour them even more than your own and keep the knowledge that they are not yours shut within you.
229.nuance: Pope's title says to love them the more; the verse says மதித்து, to value or honour.

positions.position: One is to honour them more than one's real friends, with no suggestion of pretence.
positions.quote: த‌ம‌ரினும் ந‌ன்கு ம‌தித்து - ந‌ண்ப‌ரினும் மிக‌க் கௌர‌வித்து

positions.position: The honour is an outward show while the truth is kept inside.
positions.quote: தம் உறவினரினும் நன்கு மதிப்பது போல் வெளிக்குக் காட்டி

230.reading: If, after taking someone as my friend, I go about searching out his faults and his other qualities, may I go where the man who did not guard his friend's secret goes, while the world encircled by the roaring sea laughs.
230.nuance: A curse spoken in the first person. Mudaliar names the destination as hell. Examining a friend belongs before the friendship (chapter 22); after it, examining is treated as betrayal.

links.note: 75 says to bear a friend's unkind conduct as far as one can and, if one cannot, to withdraw without speaking ill. 221 offers no such exit: keep them and keep their faults inside.
Both ask for a charitable account of a friend's wrongs. 805 says to put them down to folly or great intimacy; 221 says every good thing has its husk.
Both make forbearance toward those who damage you an image from the land: the earth bears those who dig into it (151), and the farmer re-dams the stream that keeps breaking through (222).
803 asks what use an old friendship is if one doesn't accept a friend's liberties as one's own acts. 223 puts the same demand as a maxim: one person's patience keeps two in friendship.
Both picture a wrong friendship as burning the heart. In 799 it is the memory of friends who deserted one; in 224 it is a friend one cannot leave who lacks good nature.
Adjacent quatrains turn fire both ways: in 224 a bad friend is a fire lit to burn the heart, and in 225 the fire that burned the house is still needed daily, so the friend who hurt one is kept.
Both forbid casting off a close friend for the hurt they cause. 76 says to blame oneself, since even beasts find parting hard; 226 says no one cuts off the hand that poked their eye.
980 says greatness hides others' faults and smallness only tells them. 227 applies this to friends and ranks the teller below the wrongdoer.
188 asks what those who spread the faults of their intimates would do to strangers. 227 makes the same judgement on those who publish a friend's wrongs.
Both reinterpret a friend's hurtful act. 805 reads it as folly or intimacy; 228 says it becomes good once held in the heart.

830 says to befriend a former enemy with the face, let go in the heart, and then drop the friendship. 229 also hides an inner judgement behind outward regard, but toward a friend who has proved false, and it never says to drop him.

504 tells one to examine a person's qualities and faults and take what predominates. 230 forbids that examination once the friendship is made, so the two divide the labour: examine before, never after.

Both are first-person curses with the same frame: may I go where the worst betrayer of a friend goes, while the world laughs. 230 names the one who did not keep a friend's secret, and 238 the one who violated a friend's wife.

source_issues: 221 to 228: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
223: the shanmuganar field ends with the text of 224 and Shanmuganar's comment on it; 224's own shanmuganar field is not aligned.
224, 226 and 229: the Tamil has a corrupted character (கா஢யா, தமா஢னும்) where ரி is expected.
230: Pope's title and translation run together, and the text field is a separator line. The shanmuganar field ends with the header of chapter 24.
